findings.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 — [P1, confidence 100] `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` compares the raw signup value although the application canonicalizes emails with `Email.downcase` elsewhere, so case/whitespace variants of one logical address create separate policy identities and a blocked address is not consistently rejected.

app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — [P2, confidence 100] `record.match_count += 1` followed by `record.save` is a read-modify-write counter update, so concurrent validations overwrite one another and `match_count` permanently underreports matched addresses.

goldens.comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.

The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb:5 — [P2, confidence 100] `t.integer :action_type, null: false` neither constrains the enum nor supplies its declared default, so invalid persisted action values are silently treated as `:do_nothing` and non-ActiveRecord writers cannot create the model's default state.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real architectural concern: the migration creates action_type as NOT NULL without a database-level default, while the model sets defaults via before_validation callback. This means non-ActiveRecord writers (direct SQL, other services) cannot create records without explicitly specifying action_type, and there's no database constraint preventing invalid enum values. However, this is not a bug per se - the code will work correctly when used through ActiveRecord as designed. The model's set_defaults callback (line 20-22 in blocked_email.rb) handles the default, and the should_block? method (lines 11-17) correctly checks action_type. It's a valid architectural concern about database-level integrity but not a defect in the current implementation.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that `Enum` is not defined anywhere in the repository, but this diff only shows a subset of the codebase. This is a Discourse application (a well-known Rails forum software), and `Enum` is a custom class that exists in the Discourse codebase. The diff cannot prove that `Enum` doesn't exist - it simply doesn't show the file where `Enum` is defined. The code pattern `Enum.new(:block, :do_nothing)` is consistent with Discourse's custom Enum implementation. Without evidence that this actually fails, this is speculation about code outside the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:8 — [P1, confidence: 100] `@actions ||= Enum.new(:block, :do_nothing)` raises an unhandled `NameError` whenever an existing blocked-email record is evaluated (or a new one gets its default), causing the signup request to return a raw 500 instead of its failure JSON contract.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that `Enum.new(:block, :do_nothing)` raises a NameError, implying the Enum class doesn't exist. However, this is a Discourse codebase (as evidenced by `Discourse.Controller.extend` in the JS files), and Discourse has its own Enum class defined elsewhere in the codebase. The diff shows this code being added and used consistently - the fabricator uses `BlockedEmail.actions[:block]`, the specs test both action types, and the model references it. If Enum didn't exist, none of the tests would pass. The finding assumes a missing dependency that isn't verifiable from the diff and contradicts the evidence that the code is being used successfully in tests.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — [P2, confidence: 100] `record.match_count += 1` followed by `record.save` performs a non-atomic read-modify-write, so simultaneous validation requests for one blocked address overwrite each other's increments and silently undercount block matches.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows in app/models/blocked_email.rb lines 12-17 that `should_block?` performs `record.match_count += 1` followed by `record.save`. This is indeed a non-atomic read-modify-write operation. If two concurrent requests validate the same blocked email, both could read the same match_count value, increment it locally, and save - resulting in only one increment being recorded instead of two. This is a real race condition bug in the newly introduced code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:12 — P2/C100: `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` performs an exact unnormalized comparison, so an unauthenticated registrant can bypass a block entry such as `blocked@example.com` by submitting a case-variant address (for example `Blocked@Example.com`).

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that BlockedEmail.should_block? uses `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` which performs an exact string comparison in the database. Looking at the diff in app/models/blocked_email.rb lines 11-17, the query `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` does not normalize the email case. If a blocked email is stored as 'blocked@example.com', a user could bypass it by registering with 'Blocked@Example.com' since SQL string comparison is typically case-sensitive by default. This is a legitimate security bypass vulnerability in the email blocking feature being introduced.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb:19 — [P3; confidence 100] `record.errors[:email].should be_present` also passes when the validator emits `user.email.not_allowed` or any unrelated email error, so the new `user.email.blocked` outcome and message are not actually verified.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a test quality issue. Looking at the test in spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb lines 15-19, the test stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? to return true and then asserts `record.errors[:email].should be_present`. However, this assertion would pass if ANY email error is added, not specifically the 'user.email.blocked' error. The EmailValidator in lib/validators/email_validator.rb can add either 'user.email.not_allowed' (from whitelist/blacklist checks) or 'user.email.blocked' (from BlockedEmail check). The test doesn't verify the specific error message, so it doesn't actually confirm the blocked email path adds the correct error. This is a legitimate test coverage gap for newly added logic.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the new email_validator_spec.rb only tests the BlockedEmail blocking functionality but does not test the whitelist/blacklist logic that was moved from user.rb to the new EmailValidator class. Looking at the diff, the validator at lib/validators/email_validator.rb:4-11 contains the refactored whitelist/blacklist logic, but the spec file only has tests for 'blocked email' context with no tests for email_domains_whitelist or email_domains_blacklist settings. This is a legitimate test coverage gap for newly refactored code - the logic was moved but the tests for that specific logic were not added to the new validator spec.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/users_controller.rb:198 — [P2; confidence 100] No added test drives a blocked email through `UsersController#create` and asserts `errors: user.errors.to_hash` plus `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")`, so an incompatible failure payload that prevents `create_account_controller.js:274` from rejecting the submitted address will still pass the new isolated model and validator specs.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that while the diff adds new functionality for handling blocked emails (BlockedEmail model, EmailValidator, and client-side rejection tracking), there is no integration test that verifies the full flow through UsersController#create. The diff shows: 1) UsersController#create now returns `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice(...)` on failure (lines 196-199), 2) The JavaScript relies on this structure at line 274 to push rejected emails, 3) The new specs only test the model (blocked_email_spec.rb) and validator (email_validator_spec.rb) in isolation. A controller spec testing the blocked email scenario through the full request/response cycle is indeed missing, which could allow regressions in the JSON response format to go undetected.
